catalog_quote: Described in this section are the major prosodic patterns observed in utterances consisting of simple declarative clauses ending in a verb. ... The pitch track shows a gentle decline in pitch across the utterance, from a peak in ditsǫǫ xah 'for his own grandmother'. The lowest pitch can be found on the pre-stem syllable, with a very slight rise toward the stem syllable. [p. 194:] This pattern of gently declining pitch with very slight stem stress is very common in the Tetlin dialect, where there is no low tone. Figure 11.2 shows the wave form and pitch track of (263), produced by a male speaker of the Tetlin dialect. The peak in this utterance is the directional stem, which bears the high tone typical of these lexical items (see vol. 1, chap. 17). ... In the tonal Northway dialect this pattern is just as commonly found when the stem syllable is not tonally marked. ... The low tone on the pre-stem syllable exacerbates the rise on the stem syllable. [p. 195:] Another common pattern in both dialects is to extend the falling pitch onto the verb stem.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Upper Tanana is described as a tone language (unmarked vs. low-marked vs. high-marked syllables; Lovick 2020: 72), and Lovick's two-volume reference grammar contains no section on word stress: a full-text search of Vol. 1 finds 'stress' exactly once and 'stressed/unstressed/accent/prominence' never, and Vol. 1 p. 84 defers 'utterance prosody' to Vol. 2. What the primary sources do say is that the stem (root) syllable -- the final syllable of the prefixing verb/noun word -- carries a weak prominence: Lovick 2023: 193-194 describes declaratives with a pitch minimum on the pre-stem syllable and a slight rise/'very slight stem stress' on the stem syllable, and Minoura 1994: 178 likewise presupposes 'the stem stress' (Nabesna dialect, 'resembling.. toneless Ahtna'). I.e. weak morphologically located (stem = word-final root syllable) prominence in a low-marked tone language; no syllable-counting rule is given anywhere.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Lovick 2020: 265 (ch. 18): the closed class of nine adjectives (abah 'ouch', elih 'cold', elok 'hot', idzii' 'scary', įįjih 'forbidden', teejuh 'poor thing', etc.) are 'disyllabic with the stress on the second syllable' and mostly unrelated to other stems -- the only use of the word 'stress' in Vol. 1 (seen as a Google Books snippet; p. 265 itself is outside the preview). Directional stems and negative verb stems bear lexical high/extra-high tone (Lovick 2020 ch. 7, 17; Lovick & Tuttle 2011: 133), which produces the utterance pitch peak independent of 'stress'.
new_statements.domain_note: The quoted statement is about utterance-level prosody of verb-final declarative clauses (Tetlin and Northway dialects), not a citation-form word-stress rule; 'stem stress' is mentioned in passing and characterised as 'very slight'. The Vol. 1 phonology chapters (tone, syllable structure, light/heavy stems) were checked via preview pages and exhaustive full-text term search and contain no word-stress description. A catalog entry should read: tone language (low-marked; Tetlin has lost low tone); weak stem(-final) prominence noted; no dedicated stress description.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Upper Tanana proper (uppe1437, ISO tau). Lovick's prosody data are from the Tetlin (T; low tone lost) and Northway (N; tonal) dialects; Minoura's 'stem stress' remark concerns the Nabesna dialect; Scottie Creek/Beaver Creek (Canada) retain tone best. No separate Glottolog dialect codes were used.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Scan without text layer, scanned (22 pp). Sec. 1.1.3 Tones (p.169-170): 'Upper Tanana is a low-toned language'; unmarked high vs marked low tone, plus 'super-high' tone in the Canadian dialect. The only stress mention is p.178 (sec. 2.2), about the Nabesna dialect: original stem tones unclear, which 'may be accounted for by the dynamic intonational phenomena related to the stem stress, resembling those of the neighboring toneless Ahtna, which, in NB, affects the steady register tones and obscures the original tones.' No stress rule stated; 'stem stress' presupposed.
